title: The R&D Refund Gap: Why a Biotech or Medtech Scaleup's Runway Rarely Matches Its Burn Rate
linkedin:
A biotech or medtech scaleup can do everything right and still misjudge its own runway.

Here's the mechanism we keep seeing: the R&D Tax Incentive is one of the best non-dilutive funding sources available to an early-stage life sciences business. But the refund doesn't arrive when the spend happens. It's calculated through the annual tax return, so the cash can land many months after the trial costs, prototype work and contract research it's meant to offset.

Most founders count that refund the moment the spend qualifies, not the moment it actually clears the bank account. That gap sits quietly in the runway model until the business is tight on cash, and then it becomes the difference between raising on your own timeline and raising because the bank balance made the decision for you.

Investors already draw this line in due diligence. They separate confirmed cash from anticipated cash before they look at anything else. A founder who has done the same internally negotiates from strength. One who hasn't tends to discover the gap during the investor's own diligence, which is a far harder place to find it.

The fix isn't complicated. Run two lines in the forecast every week: cash actually confirmed, and cash reasonably expected but not yet cleared. Make hiring, trial timing and raise decisions off the first line only.

A note for East Coast business owners running a biotech, medtech or life sciences scaleup: the R&D Tax Incentive is one of the strongest funding tools available to your business, but it can quietly distort how much cash runway you think you have.

The refund is calculated through your annual tax return, which means it typically lands many months after the trial costs, prototype work or contract research it's meant to offset. If your cash flow forecast counts that refund the moment the spend qualifies, rather than the moment the money actually clears your account, your real runway is shorter than the numbers suggest.

This matters most in the lead-up to a capital raise. Investors and lenders separate confirmed cash from anticipated refunds as one of their first steps in due diligence. Businesses that haven't done the same internally often find themselves negotiating from a weaker position than they need to.

The practical fix is straightforward: track confirmed cash and anticipated cash as two separate lines in your weekly forecast, and make hiring, trial and raise-timing decisions off the confirmed line only.
